newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends mostly higher in US, but sterling reigns.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends mostly higher in US, but sterling reigns.

text.p: The dollar rose against the mark and yen on Tuesday despite fresh complaints from U.S. businesses that a strong U.S. currency will hurt the economy.
But market attention was focused on the pound's continued advance against the mark and dollar, amid expectations that sterling's attractive investment returns will get richer.

"Other than that, it's been kind of a quiet day. There have been some bearish (dollar) comments that really had no effect on the dollar," said Mark Remigio, a vice president at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi, in New York.

Jerry Jasinowski, head of the National Association of Manufacturers, said on Tuesday he expected the Clinton administration to tone down its support for a strong dollar as U.S. economic growth slows in 1997.
His remarks echoed protests earlier this year by several major U.S. manufacturers, notably the big-three auto makers.
"The current level of the dollar is preventing the expected boom in U.S. exports from occurring," he said.
A strong dollar makes U.S. products costlier overseas.
The dollar rose to 111.56/61 yen from 111.30/35 yen at the open and to 1.5054/57 marks, from 1.5024/29 marks.
The pound rose to a fresh four-year high at $1.6769 early Tuesday and set a 30-month high at 2.5231 marks in U.S. trade. It ended at $1.6752/62, up slightly from its $1.6751/56 open.
Investors have been flocking to the pound since the British government made U.K. investments more attractive by increasing interest rates late last month.
Upcoming data are expected to show the U.K. economy remains robust, while persistent signs of inflation pressures are keeping hopes for another Bank of England rate increase alive, traders said.

"Same story--people think you are going to see a rate hike potentially at the (next) monetary meeting," said Anne Pankowski, a vice president at Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, in New York. "There is no reason for the trend in sterling to have stalled out yet."

For the second day, the dollar dipped below 1.50 marks in Europe, due in part to reported investor demand for the German currency on the initial stock offering of Deutsche Telekom AG on Monday, traders said.

Demand from investors around the world reportedly outstripped available shares by a huge margin, even though the German telecommunications giant decided last week to up its offering by 213 million shares.
"I tend to think now that the share flotation is out of the way, maybe you are going to alleviate some of the selling pressure on dollar/mark," Pankowski said.

Mark buying petered out in U.S. trading and the dollar got a late day lift after U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin signalled he would keep his job in the second four years of the Clinton administration.

Rubin continues to state the administration's support for a strong dollar, saying it is in America's interest. Despite frequent complaints by exporters, he has rejected suggestions that Washington use the currency as a trade tool.
Overall, dollar trade was subdued before Wednesday's 0830 EST/1330 GMT release of U.S. September international trade data, dealers said.

In other trade, the dollar rose to 1.2715/25 Swiss francs from 1.2680/85 Swiss at the open. It fell to Canadian $1.3418/23 from C$1.3439/44. The Australian dollar rose to $0.7943/48 from $0.7938/43. -- Alden Bentley 212 859 1667
